A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same synthetic-data framework and recommendation scaling study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-versus-real training comparisons, Qwen3 scaling experiments, data-mixture ablations, and appendix experiments on random-walk configurations and semantic tokenization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds joint scaling fits, results on proprietary social-media data with Gemma 3 and Qwen3, and a bias audit.

M1.justification: The item-text/CF curriculum, graph-based UIH generation, and CPT procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B's opening now correctly identifies SAE as the selected tokenizer, matching the selection already stated in v1 Section B.2. This correction does not establish a method change.

E1.justification: Section 9.1 adds experiments on a proprietary social-media recommendation dataset, extending coverage beyond MerRec e-commerce and the retained general-language corpus. This is a substantive new application domain.

E2.justification: The evaluated GRU4Rec, NARM, STAMP, SASRec, random-walk variants, and tokenizer comparisons are retained. GLTA and S-Walk are added only to related work. Gemma 3 supplies another model family using the framework, rather than a competing recommendation method.

E3.justification: The added social-media experiments introduce Gemma 3 configurations of 1B, 4B, and 12B, Qwen3 configurations through 30B-A3B, and a reported Qwen3-4B budget extension from 163B to 1,104B tokens. Section 9.2 also reports evaluating perplexity against Recall@K/NDCG. The original MerRec settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 6.2.2 adds joint model-size/data fitting and domain-specific compute-allocation analysis beyond v1's per-model fits and endpoint compute analysis. Appendix C adds an explicit bias audit using the existing 14 random-walk configurations; its Gini and item-count ranges largely reuse Appendix A. Existing ablations and case studies remain.

E5.justification: v3 adds joint statistical estimation of model-size/data scaling parameters and reports fit RMSE below 0.035 for the social-media experiments. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The RMSE reporting measures fit quality, not uncertainty across training runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds joint-fit coefficients and Gemma 3 results, including UIH exponents of 0.274, 0.237, and 0.205 for 1B, 4B, and 12B models in Table 9. It also reports continued scaling to 1,104B tokens and a downstream-metric correlation without numerical correlation values. Original result tables remain; Figure 2's caption changes its UIH exponent range from 0.63–0.99 to 0.45–0.59.

T1.justification: The joint power-law form already appears in v1 Equation 1. v3 adds mathematical reasoning under C = 6ND, including the optimality condition αA N^(-α) = βB D^(-β) and data multipliers needed to halve a loss component. The fitted numerical equations are primarily empirical additions; no new theorem or proof framework appears.

C1.justification: The central claims about synthetic-data utility, recommendation scaling laws, and asymmetric CF-to-UIH transfer remain. The introduction narrows one contribution from eliminating position and popularity biases to eliminating positional and presentation-order artifacts, replacing the broader 'unbiased' characterization.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges retained popularity bias, develops model-capacity versus data-coverage interpretations, and notes interactions missed by the additive joint fit. Sections 9.2–9.3 add arguments about downstream relevance and denoising versus distributional simplicity. Some interpretations are inconsistent with the evidence: Table 9 does not support Section 9.1's claim that exponents decrease with model size in every domain.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies 100K sequences per random-walk configuration and asserts training-only graph construction, nonoverlapping UIH sequences, and evaluation-only use of test graph structure. Its additional assertion that SAE training uses only training-split item descriptions is not reconciled with Appendix B's internally pretrained multimodal SAE description. These disclosures do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: Section 2.4 adds GLTA and S-Walk citations and distinguishes their approaches from the proposed data curriculum. Section 2.2 expands comparisons with generative augmentation, sequence perturbation, and sample-level LLM generation. The broader data-centric positioning and existing literature coverage remain.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted rewrites in related work, scaling analysis, and discussion; subdivides Sections 6.2 and 9; and adds Appendix C. It also corrects tokenizer-selection wording, narrows bias terminology, and updates authors/publication information. Most existing prose and the overall narrative order are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 4, 9, and 12 for compute trade-offs, Gemma results, and the bias audit. Existing tables are renumbered, and retained figures shift with pagination. The twelve figure graphics remain, with caption corrections including Figure 2's exponent range and Figure 12's SAE-versus-RQ-kmeans comparison.

improvement.justification: v3 provides broader empirical coverage, more useful scaling analysis, and a clearer acknowledgment that popularity bias persists. It also corrects misleading tokenizer and figure descriptions. These gains are limited by sparse documentation of the proprietary experiments and new inconsistencies: Section 9.1 contradicts Table 9's exponent trends, while Appendix C.2's SAE-training assertion remains unreconciled with Appendix B. Overall, the additions improve the paper modestly, with limited confidence in some new conclusions.
